articles.title: Personalized brain therapy hits 68 percent remission for PTSD
articles.summary:
Image alt text: Patient receiving transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy for PTSD treatment in a clinical setting A newly FDA-cleared treatment for PTSD reported 68 percent remission in clinical trials. The best-performing approved medications for the condition top out at around 10.9 percent. The treatment, called Magnetic e-Resonance Therapy (MeRT), was developed by California-based Wave Neuroscience […]
The post Personalized brain therapy hits 68 percent remission for PTSD first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
Image alt text: Patient receiving transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy for PTSD treatment in a clinical setting

A newly FDA-cleared treatment for PTSD reported 68 percent remission in clinical trials. The best-performing approved medications for the condition top out at around 10.9 percent.

The treatment, called Magnetic e-Resonance Therapy (MeRT), was developed by California-based Wave Neuroscience in collaboration with researchers at the Texas A&M Health Institute of Biosciences and Technology. It pairs brain activity mapping with personalized magnetic stimulation. The clinical trial also reported a 52 percent reduction in PTSD symptoms overall.

“Our FDA trial reported a 52 percent reduction in symptoms, so more than a four-fold increase in efficacy,” said Erik Won, D.O., Wave Neuroscience’s chief medical officer. “And more importantly, we saw 68 percent remission in our clinical trial. From a clinical care perspective, that’s really meaningful.” These results come from different studies, not a direct head-to-head comparison, but the gap is hard to ignore.

How MeRT personalizes treatment

The process starts with an electroencephalogram (EEG) that records each patient’s brain electrical activity. An AI-assisted algorithm uses that data to build a personalized stimulation plan. A coil placed against the scalp then delivers targeted magnetic pulses through transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), a technique already FDA-cleared for treatment-resistant depression.

Standard TMS follows a generalized protocol. MeRT adjusts based on what’s happening in each patient’s brain. Dr. Kenneth S. Ramos, a precision medicine researcher at Texas A&M Health who helped guide the study, put it this way: standard TMS covers the leak with a tarp; MeRT tries to find and replace the damaged shingles.

Participants received five sessions per week over five to six weeks, but improvements appeared to persist after the sessions ended.

The first FDA-cleared non-drug option for PTSD

PTSD was formally recognized as a diagnosis in 1980. Since then, treatment has relied on two FDA-approved medications, both SSRIs, and psychotherapy. A 2020 review found medication remission rates reached 10.9 percent at most.

MeRT will be the first FDA-cleared non-medication treatment specifically for PTSD. Dr. Israel Liberzon, the study’s lead psychiatrist and a distinguished professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at the Texas A&M Naresh K. Vashisht College of Medicine, explained what that means for patients. “Right now, the FDA has approved only two medications for PTSD,” he said. “This is the first time that in addition to the medication, we have a non-medication option. There is psychotherapy that people use for PTSD, but psychotherapies require a lot of effort. People must participate actively, and many drop out because it’s too anxiety provoking. So now we have a unique alternative.”

About six percent of Americans will experience PTSD during their lifetime, with higher rates among women and veterans. In the United States, approximately 17.5 veterans die by suicide each day.

“People living with PTSD have been left with trial-and-error treatment, medications and their side effects, and limited outcomes—even when treated by the most dedicated and experienced physicians,” Won said. “Wave’s FDA clearance signals a fundamentally different future: one in which PTSD can be objectively evaluated, precisely treated and meaningfully healed.”

Wave Neuroscience and Texas A&M Health are working on insurance coverage to make the therapy more widely accessible. Won also believes MeRT could eventually be adapted for depression, anxiety, and other psychiatric conditions.
articles.source: The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News

It offers a meaningful, scalable treatment alternative for millions affected by PTSD, including veterans, with detailed clinical trial results and expert commentary, highlighting a major breakthrough in mental health treatment.

articles.title: AI helps Stanford scientists discover a “natural Ozempic” with a surprising advantage
articles.summary: Stanford researchers have discovered an AI-identified natural molecule that dramatically suppresses appetite and promotes fat loss in animals, potentially offering an Ozempic-like weight-loss treatment without common digestive side effects or significant muscle loss. Called BRP, the molecule reduced food intake by up to 50% and targets a different brain pathway, raising hopes for a more precise obesity treatment if future human trials prove successful.
articles.content:
Scientists at Stanford Medicine have identified a naturally occurring molecule that could lead to a new generation of weight loss medications. Early animal experiments suggest that it can suppress appetite and promote fat loss much like semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic, while potentially avoiding some of the drug's troublesome side effects.

The molecule, known as BRP, works differently from existing treatments. Rather than affecting several organs throughout the body, it appears to act more selectively on a part of the brain responsible for controlling hunger and metabolism. This more focused approach could eventually help people lose weight without experiencing problems such as nausea, constipation, or substantial muscle loss.

Researchers discovered BRP with the help of artificial intelligence, which allowed them to search through thousands of possible biological compounds. The findings were promising enough that the scientists began preparing for the next major step: determining whether the molecule is safe and effective in humans.

"The receptors targeted by semaglutide are found in the brain but also in the gut, pancreas and other tissues," said assistant professor of pathology Katrin Svensson, PhD. "That's why Ozempic has widespread effects including slowing the movement of food through the digestive tract and lowering blood sugar levels. In contrast, BRP appears to act specifically in the hypothalamus, which controls appetite and metabolism."

A Different Approach to Weight Loss

The hypothalamus is a small but essential region deep within the brain. Among its many responsibilities, it helps regulate hunger, energy use, body temperature, and other functions needed to maintain the body's internal balance. Because it plays such a central role in appetite, it is an important target for researchers developing obesity treatments.

Semaglutide works by imitating a hormone called glucagon-like peptide 1, or GLP-1. This hormone helps regulate blood sugar and signals that influence hunger and feelings of fullness. However, GLP-1 receptors are distributed throughout several parts of the body, which helps explain why medications that activate them can produce effects beyond appetite suppression.

BRP appears to take another route. Although it influences some of the same broad metabolic functions as semaglutide, it activates different populations of brain cells. Scientists believe this distinction could make it possible to control hunger more precisely while reducing unwanted effects elsewhere in the body.

Svensson, who served as senior author of the study, published in Nature, has also cofounded a company to advance BRP toward human clinical trials. The research was led by senior research scientist Laetitia Coassolo, PhD.

How Artificial Intelligence Uncovered a Hidden Molecule

Finding BRP required solving a problem that has long complicated the search for new hormones. The human body produces enormous numbers of small protein fragments, but only a fraction have important biological functions. Identifying the ones that influence appetite or metabolism can be extremely difficult.

Many hormones begin as larger, inactive proteins known as prohormones. Specialized enzymes cut these proteins into smaller pieces called peptides. Some of those peptides become chemical messengers that help coordinate processes such as energy metabolism, appetite, and organ function.

A single prohormone can be cut in several different places, potentially producing numerous peptides with distinct effects. The challenge is determining which fragments are biologically useful and which are simply leftovers from normal protein processing. The important peptide hormones (which are relatively rare) can be difficult to distinguish from the much larger collection of ordinary protein fragments.

Traditional approaches often involve extracting proteins from biological tissues and analyzing them with techniques such as mass spectrometry. This method identifies molecules by measuring characteristics related to their mass, but the sheer number of possible peptides makes searching for new hormones a demanding process.

The Stanford team decided to approach the problem differently. They concentrated on an enzyme called prohormone convertase 1/3, which cuts prohormones at particular amino acid sequences and has previously been linked to human obesity. Amino acids are the molecular building blocks of proteins, and their arrangement helps determine where enzymes can cut them.

One of the hormones produced through this process is GLP-1, the same hormone whose effects semaglutide mimics. The researchers reasoned that other peptides generated through similar processing might also help regulate appetite and energy use.

AI Searches 20,000 Human Genes for New Hormones

To accelerate the search, the scientists created a computer algorithm called Peptide Predictor. Instead of physically isolating and examining hundreds of thousands of peptides, the program analyzed the roughly 20,000 genes that encode human proteins, looking for sequences where the enzyme was likely to make cuts.

The team then refined the results by concentrating on genes associated with proteins released outside cells, a common characteristic of hormones. They also required each candidate protein to contain at least four potential cutting sites.

These filters reduced an enormous collection of possibilities to 373 prohormones, making experimental testing much more practical.

"The algorithm was absolutely key to our findings," Svensson said.

Peptide Predictor estimated that the enzyme could produce 2,683 distinct peptides from those 373 proteins. From this collection, Svensson and Coassolo selected candidates that appeared particularly likely to influence brain activity.

The researchers eventually tested 100 peptides, including GLP-1, using nerve cells grown in the laboratory. Their goal was to find substances capable of stimulating neuronal activity, an early indication that a peptide might influence important brain processes.

A Tiny Peptide Produces a Surprising Result

GLP-1 performed strongly in the laboratory tests, increasing neuronal activity to three times the level observed in untreated control cells.

One previously unrecognized peptide, however, produced an even more striking response. Consisting of just 12 amino acids, it increased neuronal activity tenfold compared with the controls.

The researchers named the molecule BRP after the larger protein from which it originates, BPM/retinoic acid inducible neural specific 2, or BRINP2 (BRINP2-related-peptide).

That unusually powerful response made BRP a promising candidate for further investigation. The next question was whether stimulating laboratory-grown brain cells would translate into meaningful changes in appetite and body weight in living animals.

Food Intake Drops by Up to 50% in Animal Experiments

The team tested BRP in lean mice and minipigs (which more closely mirror human metabolism and eating patterns than mice do). Before the animals were fed, researchers administered BRP through an injection into the muscle.

The results were striking. During the following hour, the treated animals consumed up to 50% less food than expected, suggesting that BRP could strongly influence hunger.

The scientists then examined whether repeated treatment could produce sustained changes in body weight. Obese mice received daily BRP injections for 14 days. By the end of the experiment, the treated mice had lost an average of 3 grams, while untreated control mice had gained approximately 3 grams.

Importantly, nearly all the weight lost by the BRP-treated mice came from body fat rather than muscle. Preserving muscle is an important goal in obesity treatment because muscle tissue supports strength, mobility, and metabolic health.

The treated animals also showed improvements in glucose and insulin tolerance. These measurements reflect how effectively the body handles sugar and responds to insulin, the hormone that helps move glucose from the bloodstream into cells.

Together, the findings suggest that BRP may influence both appetite and metabolic health, although it remains unknown whether people would experience comparable benefits.

Could BRP Avoid Common Ozempic Side Effects?

One of the most intriguing aspects of the discovery is the possibility that BRP could provide weight loss benefits while avoiding some unwanted effects associated with semaglutide and similar medications.

To investigate potential side effects, the researchers monitored the behavior and physical responses of the treated mice and pigs. They found no significant differences in movement, water consumption, anxiety-related behavior, or fecal output compared with control animals.

The absence of changes in fecal production was particularly interesting because constipation is a known side effect of medications such as Ozempic. The experiments also showed that BRP promoted fat loss without the substantial muscle loss that can accompany some weight reduction treatments.

Nausea is another common concern with existing GLP-1 medications, although animal experiments cannot fully establish whether BRP would prevent that symptom in people. Human testing will be essential to determine the molecule's actual side effect profile.

Additional investigations into brain activity and other physiological responses reinforced the idea that BRP works differently from semaglutide. The peptide activated distinct neuronal and metabolic pathways rather than simply copying the effects of GLP-1.

This difference may explain why the researchers observed strong appetite suppression without several of the behavioral and digestive changes they were monitoring.

What Comes Next for the Potential Ozempic Alternative?

Despite the encouraging findings, BRP is still at an early stage of development. Researchers need to understand more about exactly how the molecule communicates with cells and how its effects might be sustained over longer periods.

One priority is identifying the cell surface receptors that recognize BRP. Receptors are specialized proteins that respond to particular chemical signals, allowing cells to detect messages and trigger appropriate biological responses. Determining which receptors BRP activates could help explain its effects on hunger and metabolism.

The team also wants to investigate ways of extending the molecule's activity inside the body. Peptides can be broken down relatively quickly, potentially requiring frequent injections. A longer-lasting version of BRP could make treatment more convenient if it eventually proves effective in people.

The ultimate challenge will be establishing whether its apparent advantages in animals translate into meaningful benefits for patients. Clinical trials will need to evaluate its safety, effectiveness, appropriate dosage, and potential side effects before it could become a practical obesity treatment.

"The lack of effective drugs to treat obesity in humans has been a problem for decades," Svensson said. "Nothing we've tested before has compared to semaglutide's ability to decrease appetite and body weight. We are very eager to learn if it is safe and effective in humans."

Research Collaborators and Funding

Scientists from the University of California, Berkeley; the University of Minnesota; and the University of British Columbia also participated in the research.

Financial support came from the National Institutes of Health (grants R01DK125260, P30DK116074, K99AR081618 and GM113854), the SPARK Translational Research Program at Stanford, Stanford Bio-X, the Stanford Maternal and Child Health Research Institute, the American Heart Association, a Stanford Medicine Dean's Fellowship Award, the Carlsberg Foundation, and the Wu Tsai Human Performance Alliance.

Svensson and Coassolo are named inventors on patents involving the use of BRP peptides to treat metabolic disorders. Svensson is also a cofounder of Merrifield Therapeutics.

articles.title: A surprising discovery could help aging muscles repair themselves
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered a compound that transforms a natural muscle-repair protein into a more powerful version dubbed "Super HGF," more than doubling its ability to bind to a key receptor while protecting it from age-related chemical damage. The breakthrough, supported by early mouse experiments, could eventually help combat muscle loss and preserve strength as people age.
articles.content:
Muscles can begin losing their strength and ability to recover surprisingly early in the aging process. Over time, muscle tissue may develop scar tissue, accumulate fat, and lose some of the specialized fibers responsible for rapid, powerful movements. These changes can make everyday activities more difficult and gradually reduce mobility and physical independence.

Now, scientists in Japan have identified a promising molecule that could help protect the body's natural muscle repair system and potentially make it more effective. In laboratory experiments, the compound strengthened an important biological signal involved in muscle regeneration, increasing its ability to connect with a key cellular receptor by more than twofold.

The discovery comes from a team led by Professor Ryuichi Tatsumi at Kyushu University's Faculty of Agriculture. Their findings, published in Scientific Reports, suggest a possible new approach to addressing the cellular changes that make aging muscles increasingly difficult to repair.

How Aging Disrupts the Body's Muscle Repair System

Skeletal muscles are the muscles attached to bones that allow us to walk, lift objects, maintain posture, and perform other voluntary movements. Although these muscles experience wear and tear throughout life, they also have a remarkable ability to repair themselves.

Much of that repair depends on specialized stem cells known as satellite cells. These cells normally remain inactive, positioned alongside muscle fibers until they receive a signal that repair or regeneration is needed. Once activated, they can multiply and develop into muscle cells that help restore damaged tissue.

An essential part of this process involves a protein called hepatocyte growth factor, or HGF. Despite its name, HGF plays important roles beyond the liver, including helping activate the stem cells responsible for muscle regeneration.

Under normal conditions, HGF is stored within the supportive material surrounding muscle fibers. When muscles experience an injury or mechanical stimulation, such as physical movement or stretching, the protein can be released.

HGF then attaches to a receptor called c-met on the surface of satellite cells. Receptors are specialized proteins that receive molecular signals and trigger responses inside cells. In this case, the interaction helps awaken dormant satellite cells, allowing them to multiply, mature, and participate in repairing muscle fibers.

But this carefully coordinated system becomes less reliable with age.

A Hidden Chemical Change May Weaken Aging Muscles

The researchers' previous work revealed that HGF can undergo a chemical modification known as nitration. This process attaches a chemical group called a nitro group to particular locations on a protein, potentially changing its structure and interfering with its normal activity.

For HGF, the researchers identified two especially important locations, Y198 and Y250. Both lie within the region involved in attaching to the c-met receptor.

When these sites undergo nitration, HGF becomes less capable of connecting with its receptor. The result is similar to a key that has become damaged and can no longer operate its intended lock.

This disruption could have important consequences for aging muscles. Even if the body continues producing HGF, chemical changes may prevent the protein from properly activating the stem cells needed for tissue repair. The researchers believe this mechanism may contribute to age-related muscle wasting and declining regenerative capacity.

"HGF is not necessarily missing as we age," explains Tatsumi. "Rather, it can be chemically altered after it is made. That led us to wonder whether a compound with strong antioxidant capacity might protect HGF, either by preventing nitration or by compensating for the functional loss it causes."

Scientists Test Two Powerful Sulfur Compounds

To investigate that possibility, the team studied two compounds with strong antioxidant properties: glutathione trisulfide (GSSSG) and lipoic acid trisulfide (LASSS).

Antioxidants can help limit certain types of chemical damage caused by reactive molecules. Such damage can interfere with proteins and other essential components of cells, particularly when the body's normal protective systems become less effective.

The two compounds belong to a chemical family called trisulfides. Their defining feature is a chain of three sulfur atoms connected to one another. This arrangement gives them unusual chemical properties, including an ability to participate in reactions involving the transfer of electrons, known as redox reactions.

Because these reactions play important roles in cellular chemistry, trisulfides have attracted growing interest as potential ingredients in new medicines.

In the first set of experiments, both compounds reduced nitration at the two vulnerable sites on HGF. However, preventing this chemical modification did not completely restore the protein's ability to attach to c-met.

The scientists therefore increased the amount of trisulfide used relative to HGF. They changed the molar ratio, which compares the number of molecules of each substance, from 1:4000 to 1:8000.

That adjustment produced an unexpected result.

An Unexpected Discovery Creates "Super HGF"

At the higher concentration, LASSS did much more than protect HGF from chemical damage. It also dramatically improved the protein's ability to bind to its receptor.

Compared with untreated HGF, the protein exposed to LASSS showed more than twice the binding affinity for c-met. In other words, it could attach to its target receptor much more strongly, potentially enhancing a critical step in the muscle repair process.

The treatment also made HGF more resistant to the loss of function caused by nitration, particularly at the Y198 site.

Notably, the effect was specific to LASSS. Although GSSSG had also reduced nitration in the earlier experiments, it did not produce the same improvement in receptor binding.

"This exceeded our expectations," comments Tatsumi. "We knew trisulfides had diverse biological functions, but we never expected that simply mixing HGF with LASSS would produce such a striking effect.

"What this tells us is that LASSS does more than simply neutralize reactive molecules. It may interact directly with HGF and induce a subtle structural change, creating an enhanced 'Super HGF' form that binds c-met more strongly and resists nitration."

The researchers suspect that LASSS interacts with HGF in a way that slightly alters the protein's three-dimensional shape. Because a protein's shape helps determine how well it interacts with other molecules, even a small structural adjustment could substantially change its activity.

The result is what the team describes as "Super HGF," a potentially enhanced form of the body's existing muscle repair signal.

Importantly, stronger receptor binding does not automatically establish that muscle regeneration itself has improved. Additional experiments will be needed to determine whether this molecular enhancement translates into better muscle healing and strength.

Mouse Experiments Reveal Promising Protection

After observing the effects in laboratory experiments, the researchers wanted to determine whether LASSS could also protect HGF inside living muscle tissue.

They used mice subjected to tail suspension, an established experimental method for studying muscle atrophy. By reducing normal weight bearing and muscle use, this technique produces some of the changes associated with prolonged inactivity, including muscle deterioration.

Mice that received LASSS before the experiment showed significantly less HGF nitration than untreated animals. This suggested that the compound's ability to protect the muscle repair protein was not limited to controlled laboratory conditions.

Once again, GSSSG failed to produce the same protective result.

These findings provide early evidence that LASSS can influence the chemical processes affecting HGF within living animals. However, the mouse experiments demonstrated protection against nitration, not that LASSS restored lost muscle mass or improved physical strength.

The researchers emphasize that studies involving aging animals are still necessary to establish the compound's effectiveness and safety in vivo, meaning within a living organism.

A Potential New Strategy Against Age-Related Muscle Loss

The discovery could eventually contribute to treatments aimed at maintaining muscle function during aging or extended periods of inactivity.

Muscle deterioration is not limited to older adults. It can also occur during prolonged bed rest or other situations in which muscles are used less frequently. When muscle repair mechanisms become impaired, recovering lost strength and function can become especially challenging.

Rather than replacing the body's natural repair machinery, the approach explored in this study seeks to protect and enhance an existing biological signal. If the benefits can be confirmed in future studies, strengthening HGF activity could become one strategy for supporting muscle regeneration.

The scientists also believe that the underlying effects of LASSS on HGF may extend across species. That raises the possibility of applications not only in human medicine but also in veterinary care, particularly for aging companion animals such as dogs and cats.

For now, the findings represent an early step toward understanding how a naturally occurring muscle repair pathway might be strengthened. Whether LASSS can safely and effectively preserve muscle function during aging remains an open question.

Still, the unexpected discovery that a sulfur-based compound can both protect and enhance a critical repair protein offers a promising direction for future research, with the long-term goal of helping people maintain mobility, independence, and a better quality of life as they grow older.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery of a compound that enhances a natural muscle repair protein, potentially addressing age-related muscle loss and preserving strength. This breakthrough has broad implications for aging populations and muscle health, supported by detailed experimental evidence and promising early results in animal models. The story is focused, substantive, and highlights a meaningful positive impact on health and quality of life.
articles.personality_title: New compound boosts muscle repair protein, offering hope for aging muscles
articles.personality_presentation:

HGF helps activate stem cells that repair muscle. LASSS not only protects HGF from damage caused by aging but also makes it bind more strongly to muscle cells, creating a “Super HGF.” Early tests in mice showed that LASSS reduced damage to HGF during muscle inactivity.

**Impact** – This discovery is important because it could lead to new treatments that help muscles repair themselves better as people age or after long periods of inactivity. Instead of replacing natural repair systems, this approach strengthens what the body already has. While the research is still early, it shows a new way to support muscle health and possibly keep people more mobile and independent.

**What's next step** – Scientists need to test whether the “Super HGF” created by LASSS actually improves muscle healing and strength in older animals and eventually in humans. articles.title: Toothbrush that emits electricity may more effectively prevent gum disease
articles.summary: A toothbrush with bristles that produce electricity as they bend has shown promise for reducing plaque and gum inflammation
articles.content:
A toothbrush with bristles that produce electricity as they bend has shown promise for reducing plaque and gum inflammation

A new and improved toothbrush could help avoid trips to the dentist Westend61/Alamy

A toothbrush that generates electricity may more effectively fight harmful bacteria, while removing plaque, than existing products. The toothbrush uses special bristles that produce electricity as they bend, triggering the formation of molecules that damage bacterial membranes. When put to the test, it led to more than twice the reduction of plaque, gum inflammation and bleeding as conventional toothbrushes.

“The concept is great,” says Nicholas Jakubovics at Newcastle University, UK, who wasn’t involved in the research. “Basically, the mechanical forces recharge the surface, so it’s really innovative. Anything that even slightly improves the way dental care works could have a benefit, because oral disease is just so widespread.”

Oral diseases, such as tooth decay, affect nearly half the global population. Brushing regularly can help remove plaque, a sticky layer of bacteria that forms on teeth. These bacteria can produce acids that cause cavities and irritate gums, sometimes leading to tooth loss.

Advertisement

But even thorough brushing can leave behind bacteria deep in plaque or between teeth, allowing colonies to grow back within hours. Researchers have previously developed toothbrushes with antibacterial metal nanoparticles, including silver and zinc, embedded in their bristles, although their long-term effectiveness is uncertain. Others have designed ionic toothbrushes that use electric currents to help loosen plaque, but they are dependent on batteries.

Now, Yanhui Lu at Peking University in China and her colleagues have turned to studies showing that so-called piezoelectric materials fight bacteria in infected wounds and medical implants. These generate electric charges under pressure, prompting Lu’s team to develop toothbrush bristles made from piezoelectric plastic.

Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter

The idea was that, as the bristles bend during brushing, they would generate electricity, triggering chemical reactions that produce molecules called reactive-oxygen species that damage bacteria, while the bristles physically remove plaque.

The researchers made two sets of bristles of different thicknesses, both of which met Chinese national standards for softness and strength. Laboratory tests confirmed the bristles generated electricity under pressure, particularly the thicker ones. The team also detected reactive-oxygen species on the brushes, which remained soft and retained their electrical properties after three months of use.

Next, the researchers exposed two common oral bacteria to their bristles and nylon ones, which are used in standard toothbrushes, in laboratory experiments, including simulated brushing movements. The thicker piezoelectric bristles were particularly effective, killing about 53 per cent of Streptococcus mutans, which causes cavities, and 78 per cent of Porphyromonas gingivalis, which contributes to gum disease, compared with just 9 and 8 per cent, respectively, for nylon bristles.

The team also grew plaque from human mouths on pieces of cow enamel and brushed them for 3 minutes. The new toothbrushes removed more than 99 per cent of the plaque, compared with about 80 per cent for conventional nylon brushes.

Finally, the team tested the toothbrushes in 109 adults with dental plaque and gum inflammation, who were randomly assigned to use either a piezoelectric or nylon toothbrush twice daily for three months. Dental examinations revealed reductions of roughly 40 per cent in plaque build-up, gum inflammation and bleeding among those using the piezoelectric brushes, compared with around 15 per cent for those using conventional brushes.

Genetic sequencing of the dental plaque from the piezoelectric group also revealed a decline in the relative abundance of harmful bacteria and an increase in some potentially beneficial bacteria.

Larger studies now need to establish whether the toothbrush actually prevents issues like cavities and tooth loss, says Jakubovics.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on a novel toothbrush using piezoelectric bristles that generate electricity to significantly reduce harmful oral bacteria, plaque, and gum inflammation. This innovation has a broad positive impact on oral health, which affects nearly half the global population. The study includes laboratory and human trials with clear, promising results, indicating a meaningful advancement in dental care with potential to improve quality of life and reduce dental disease worldwide.
articles.personality_title: New electric toothbrush design cuts plaque and gum disease more effectively
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Many people suffer from oral diseases like tooth decay and gum problems caused by bacteria in plaque. Regular brushing helps but does not always remove all harmful bacteria, especially those deep in plaque or between teeth.

**What happened** – Researchers at Peking University in China created a new toothbrush with special bristles made from piezoelectric plastic. These bristles produce electricity when bent during brushing. This electricity triggers chemical reactions that create molecules able to kill bacteria. Tests in the lab and with 109 adults showed the new toothbrush reduced plaque, gum inflammation, and bleeding much more than regular nylon toothbrushes.

**Impact** – This toothbrush technology works without batteries and kills a high percentage of bacteria that cause cavities and gum disease. It removed over 99% of plaque in lab tests, compared to 80% by normal brushes. People using it saw about 40% less plaque and gum problems, compared to 15% with usual brushes. This improvement could help millions of people keep their teeth and gums healthier.

**What's next step** – Larger studies will check if this toothbrush can actually prevent cavities and tooth loss over time. Researchers will also keep improving the bristles and testing how long they stay effective with daily use.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A toothbrush with electricity-generating bristles has shown it can remove more plaque and reduce gum disease better than regular brushes, offering a promising new way to improve oral health worldwide.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une nouvelle brosse à dents électrique réduit davantage la plaque et les maladies des gencives
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – De nombreuses personnes souffrent de maladies bucco-dentaires comme les caries et les problèmes de gencives causés par des bactéries dans la plaque dentaire. Le brossage régulier aide, mais n’élimine pas toujours toutes les bactéries, surtout celles profondes dans la plaque ou entre les dents.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs de l’Université de Pékin en Chine ont créé une nouvelle brosse à dents avec des poils en plastique piézoélectrique. Ces poils produisent de l’électricité lorsqu’ils se plient pendant le brossage. Cette électricité déclenche des réactions chimiques qui tuent les bactéries. Des tests en laboratoire et avec 109 adultes ont montré que cette brosse réduisait la plaque, l’inflammation et les saignements des gencives bien plus que les brosses à dents en nylon classiques.

**Impact** – Cette technologie fonctionne sans piles et tue un grand pourcentage des bactéries responsables des caries et des maladies des gencives. Elle a enlevé plus de 99 % de la plaque en laboratoire, contre 80 % pour les brosses normales. Les utilisateurs ont vu environ 40 % de réduction de la plaque et des problèmes de gencives, contre 15 % avec les brosses classiques. Cette amélioration pourrait aider des millions de personnes à garder leurs dents et leurs gencives en meilleure santé.

**Étape suivante** – Des études plus larges vérifieront si cette brosse à dents peut réellement prévenir les caries et la perte des dents sur le long terme. Les chercheurs continueront aussi d’améliorer les poils et de tester leur efficacité avec une utilisation quotidienne.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Une brosse à dents avec des poils qui génèrent de l’électricité a montré qu’elle pouvait enlever plus de plaque et réduire les maladies des gencives mieux que les brosses normales, offrant une nouvelle façon prometteuse d’améliorer la santé bucco-dentaire dans le monde entier.
articles.personality_title_es: Nuevo cepillo de dientes eléctrico reduce mejor la placa y las enfermedades de las encías
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Muchas personas sufren enfermedades bucales como caries y problemas en las encías causados por bacterias en la placa dental. Cepillarse regularmente ayuda, pero no siempre elimina todas las bacterias, especialmente las que están profundas en la placa o entre los dientes.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores de la Universidad de Pekín en China crearon un cepillo de dientes con cerdas hechas de plástico piezoeléctrico. Estas cerdas generan electricidad al doblarse durante el cepillado. Esta electricidad provoca reacciones químicas que matan bacterias. Pruebas en laboratorio y con 109 adultos mostraron que este cepillo redujo la placa, la inflamación y el sangrado de encías mucho más que los cepillos de nylon normales.

**Impacto** – Esta tecnología funciona sin baterías y elimina un alto porcentaje de bacterias que causan caries y enfermedades de las encías. Quitó más del 99 % de la placa en pruebas de laboratorio, comparado con el 80 % de los cepillos normales. Las personas que lo usaron vieron cerca de un 40 % menos de placa y problemas en las encías, frente al 15 % con cepillos comunes. Esta mejora podría ayudar a millones de personas a mantener sus dientes y encías más sanos.

**Próximo paso** – Se harán estudios más grandes para confirmar si este cepillo puede prevenir caries y pérdida de dientes a largo plazo. Los investigadores también seguirán mejorando las cerdas y probando cuánto tiempo duran efectivas con el uso diario.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Un cepillo de dientes con cerdas que generan electricidad ha demostrado que puede eliminar más placa y reducir enfermedades de las encías mejor que los cepillos normales, ofreciendo una forma prometedora de mejorar la salud bucal en todo el mundo.
